title: Černý conjecture
formal: Does every synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with \(n\ge1\) states have a reset word of length at most \((n-1)^2\)? The statement quantifies over all finite nonempty alphabets. A reset word sends every possible initial state to the same state, under the transition model below.
definitions: An automaton is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma,\delta)\), where \(|Q|=n\ge1\), \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet and \(\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q\) is total. Extend it to words by \(\delta(q,\epsilon)=q\) and \(\delta(q,wa)=\delta(\delta(q,w),a)\). A word \(w\) is a reset word if \(|\{\delta(q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\); its length is its number of letters. Synchronizing means that at least one reset word exists. Its final state is not prescribed. Initial and accepting states play no role, and the empty word handles \(n=1\). There is no strong-connectivity, fixed-alphabet or other structural promise. Partial or nondeterministic automata, and synchronization of only a prescribed subset of states, are different models. No time bound for constructing the word is imposed. In the context, \(T(n)\) denotes the maximum shortest-reset-word length over all such synchronizing automata with \(n\) states; duplicate letter transformations can be removed, so this maximum exists.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

progress.text: Černý constructs an n-state family with reset threshold exactly \((n- 1)^{2}\), establishing the sharp lower-bound target.
The classical Pin–Frankl compression argument gives a general cubic upper bound; the survey records \((n^{3}- n)/6- 1\) for \(n\ge 4\).
Szykuła combines compression with avoiding words to improve the long-standing leading cubic constant.
Shitov improves that argument to a leading constant approximately 0.1654; the exponent remains three.
Volkov’s updated list records established special classes and their reset-threshold bounds while keeping the general conjecture open.
Zhu reports a proof for the one-cluster subclass in a preprint. This card does not independently certify that proof or extend it to unrestricted automata.
Szykuła’s AFL 2026 survey explicitly states the general conjecture and identifies the cubic Shitov estimate as the best known unrestricted bound.

context_blocks.text: The selected binary question is the Černý conjecture. Its \((n-1)^2\) upper bound would match the classical worst-case family. A counterexample to the universal bound also answers this card; it need not determine the entire extremal function.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.
